newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Hair stylist helps Washington shed dowdy image.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Hair stylist helps Washington shed dowdy image.

text.p: Watch out New York. Move over Los Angeles. Washington is trying to shed its dowdy image and become the hair styling capital of the United States.

That, at least, is the aim of Dennis Roche, hair stylist and owner of Roche Salon. Washington is one of the few world capitals that is not also its country's fashion leader and, despite relentless reports of the city's decline, Washingtonians are among the wealthiest, best-educated and best-travelled people in the country.

Washington was a fashion centre at least once before when first lady Jackie Kennedy dazzled the world with her glamour and the capital shared in the reflected glory. But even then, Kenneth of New York styled her hair.
Roche, whose salon is located in the tony Washington Harbour complex at the edge of Georgetown, aspires to be the next Kenneth -- without moving to New York.

"Washington is notoriously looked down upon in the fashion industry ... you don't have the fashion celebrities or the entertainment celebrities. All we have is public servants, which are our ranking celebrities," said Roche, a 25-year industry veteran and a Washington native.

But that does not mean Washington hairdressers cannot go head-to-head with Manhattan's Frederic Fakkai or Cristophe of Beverly Hills, the stylist who gained notoriety by cutting President Bill Clinton's hair aboard Air Force One on the runway at Los Angeles International Airport four years ago.

The "industry is all about perception," Roche said, which is why he has gone to extra lengths to polish Washington's image. Embracing a diverse market that includes embassies, news media and international organisations, Roche has led Washington hairdressers into increasing their repertoire and skills to meet all hair types and needs.

The result is a threefold increase in major hair shows in the city in the past decade. And the industry has taken notice. Roche's chic salon, gaily decorated in the image of Canada's world-famous Cirque de Soleil, complete with tent-like dressing rooms, has been featured in high-profile publications such as Vogue, Harper's Bazaar and GQ magazine.
Washington's heightened fashion awareness has also drawn the attention of couture shops such as Maxmara, who will be holding a fashion show starring Linda Evangelista this year.

"The greatest gift to Washington, D.C., was to be able to raise the consciousness level," Roche said. "If people read about how Washington's happening, then people have to happen along with it or else it doesn't work."

Gone are the days when the capital's best stylists left because achieving recognition was virtually impossible in a city where politics and finance took priority over fashion. Now, Washington's newly made-over image is bringing them back, taste is improving and high-profile salons are moving in to claim a share.

Cristophe, who once told a reporter that "on some levels they are more stylish here," chose Washington over New York to open a salon four years ago because he was attracted to the international clientele, and he felt the market in New York was saturated.

"Washington is definitely ready for it (recognition)," said Cristophe, who has carved a niche for himself by specialising in the glamorous hair styles of the West Coast. "Our success proves it. When we opened the salon on a Monday morning our phones started ringing at 7 a.m. and didn't stop until Wednesday. It's (the salon) been one of the most successful."
Optimists say the time may be near when Washingtonians will no longer have to stand in the fashion shadow of New York.
